title: Respiratory examination after lung resection

brief.scenario: You are a core surgical trainee in the thoracic follow-up clinic. A 66-year-old patient had a right upper lobectomy eight months ago for lung cancer. They report mild stable breathlessness since surgery.
brief.task: Perform a focused respiratory examination, summarise the findings, and outline further assessment if the breathlessness worsens. An examiner will provide examination findings when you request them.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Recognise a previous thoracotomy and modified breath sounds without assuming that one lobe removed means a silent entire hemithorax.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Interpreting post-lobectomy changes as a pneumonectomy, or dismissing a new respiratory problem as expected postoperative breathlessness.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: I will confirm the operation and baseline symptoms, check comfort and oxygenation, and compare both sides before interpreting the signs.

flow: Introduce, consent, check current breathlessness and vital signs.
Inspect chest wall, symmetry, scars, breathing pattern and tracheal position.
Palpate expansion, percuss and auscultate both sides systematically.
Summarise provided findings and distinguish lobectomy from pneumonectomy.
Discuss warning signs, investigations, appropriate senior review and safety-netting.

grid.label: Introduction and consent
grid.pass: Names core surgical trainee, confirms patient and obtains consent
grid.high: Adds comfort, privacy and permission for focused exposure

grid.label: Safety and baseline
grid.borderline: Recognises breathlessness but does not check observations
grid.pass: Checks rest symptoms, RR and oxygen saturation
grid.high: Identifies change from postoperative baseline and any red flags

grid.label: Inspection
grid.pass: Examines scar, symmetry, work of breathing and trachea
grid.high: Identifies likely approach and describes expected surgical context without overinterpretation

grid.label: Palpation
grid.high: Relates right upper asymmetry to prior upper-lobe resection cautiously

grid.label: Percussion
grid.high: States a change requires correlation rather than inferring absence of whole lung

grid.label: Auscultation
grid.pass: Compares full accessible bilateral zones and identifies reduced right upper sounds
grid.high: Separates expected focal reduction from new focal signs

grid.label: Interpretation
grid.borderline: Describes altered right side but not operation extent
grid.pass: States findings consistent with previous right upper lobectomy
grid.high: Explains anatomy: lobectomy removes a lobe; pneumonectomy removes whole lung

grid.label: Assessment and escalation
grid.pass: States CXR, pulse oximetry, and medical/surgical review if deterioration
grid.high: Tailors urgency to hypoxia, fever, chest pain or acute deterioration

grid.label: Communication and finish
grid.pass: Explains findings, follow-up and new symptoms needing prompt assessment
grid.high: Uses plain language and checks patient understanding

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I’m here to check your lungs. Take your shirt off.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: You had lung surgery, so you are supposed to be breathless, aren’t you?

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: I get breathless on hills, yes.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I can see a scar on the right; that means that whole lung was taken out.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The operation note, available if requested, says right upper lobectomy.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will not check chest expansion; the scar already tells me which side was operated on.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will just tap once over the right upper chest; there is no need to compare the two sides.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I’ll just listen here near the scar.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: There are slightly reduced breath sounds in that upper zone.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: So the right lung is missing. That explains everything; I need not compare with the left.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: What if I became much more breathless tonight?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That is probably just how it will be after surgery. Mention it at your routine review.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Right pneumonectomy with normal postoperative breathlessness; discharge.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I’m the core surgical trainee. Could I confirm your name? I’d like to examine your breathing and chest; is that all right?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes, of course.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Are you struggling to breathe at the moment, or has your breathlessness changed recently?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No trouble sitting here. I get puffed on hills, but it hasn’t changed.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Any chest pain, fever, cough with sputum or blood?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No to all of those.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: What operation did you have, and when?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: They removed the top lobe of my right lung eight months ago.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would check respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, pulse, temperature and whether this is the postoperative baseline.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: RR 17, oxygen saturation 96% on air, pulse 78, afebrile.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: With permission I expose the chest appropriately. I inspect from the end and each side for distress, symmetry and scars. I note a healed right posterolateral thoracotomy scar. I check the trachea.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The trachea is central; there is no increased work of breathing.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I assess bilateral chest expansion, comparing upper and lower regions.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mildly reduced expansion over the right upper chest.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I percuss corresponding zones across both lungs.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No striking new area of stony dullness or hyperresonance.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I auscultate symmetrically front and back and listen for added sounds.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Slightly reduced breath sounds in the right upper zone; no crackles or wheeze.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: These findings fit previous right upper lobectomy; the whole right lung was not removed. I would compare with prior imaging and documented postoperative findings.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you assess a patient whose breathlessness became worse?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would repeat observations and focused examination, obtain a chest X-ray and involve the surgical or respiratory team, urgently if the patient were hypoxic or acutely unwell.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: What if I suddenly got much more breathless tonight?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That is not something to assume is normal after surgery. If severe or sudden, seek emergency assessment immediately; I would be concerned about causes such as pneumothorax, infection or pulmonary embolism depending on the symptoms. Do you understand what to watch for?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes. I would get help rather than wait.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will document the findings and compare them with your prior post-operative baseline.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I’m the core surgical trainee. I’m going to assess how both sides of your chest are moving and how air enters the lungs. May I check your identity and gain consent? I can stop at any point.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: That is fine.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Before examining, are you breathless at rest today? Has your usual exercise tolerance changed since the operation?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: No; I only get short of breath on hills and it is about the same.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any sudden chest pain, wheeze, fever, blood in the sputum, new cough or swollen painful leg?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: No, none of those.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Which operation was performed, and how long ago?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: The upper lobe on the right was removed eight months ago.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will confirm the operation from the record, compare observations with baseline and look for any immediate respiratory compromise.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: RR 17, SpO₂ 96% room air, pulse 78, normal temperature.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I expose appropriately and inspect posture, speaking comfort, respiratory effort, chest symmetry and scars from the front and back. If there is no thoracotomy scar, I would look for small VATS port scars under the arm or below the shoulder blade.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Healed right posterolateral thoracotomy scar; no distress.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I check tracheal position and then compare upper and lower chest expansion rather than treating the operated side as entirely absent.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Central trachea, modest right upper-zone reduction of movement.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Percussing matching zones on each side, I am checking for unexpected asymmetry that might need imaging.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: No new markedly abnormal percussion note.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I listen over matched anterior, lateral and posterior fields, including the bases, and check for focal crackles or wheeze.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Slight reduction in breath sounds at right upper zone only; no added sounds.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: My summary is a stable patient with examination features compatible with prior right upper lobectomy. The scar indicates access and the reduced local movement is plausible after resection. A pneumonectomy would mean removal of the entire right lung; I would not infer that from this scar.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The patient asks whether these signs mean lung cancer has returned.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: These examination findings alone cannot establish recurrence; I would review the planned oncological follow-up and imaging. I would be careful not to offer false reassurance or imply a diagnosis.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: What if I suddenly got much more breathless tonight?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A sudden change warrants emergency assessment, especially if there is chest pain, hypoxia or collapse. We would reassess observations and investigate, including chest radiography, with urgent senior review. That is different from your stable, longstanding hill-related symptoms.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I understand the difference.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would document exactly what I found, check old operative notes and images, and communicate any new concern clearly to the thoracic team.

failures.move: Incorrectly asserts the entire lung was removed, despite a recorded upper lobectomy
Dismisses sudden severe breathlessness as routine recovery
failures.consequence: risks delayed recognition of a new emergency.

failures.move: Starts examining without asking about breathlessness at rest or checking oxygen saturation

recovery.when: If you summarised it as a pneumonectomy
recovery.line: I need to correct my summary: the operation was an upper lobectomy, not a pneumonectomy; I will verify the operation record.

recovery.when: If you treated a new change in breathing as stable postoperative limitation
recovery.line: A new change in breathing is different from stable postoperative limitation. I would reassess observations and escalate now.

knowledge.fact: A lobectomy removes one lobe; a pneumonectomy removes an entire lung.
A thoracotomy commonly involves an incision along the side of the chest below the shoulder blade.
Breathlessness can persist after lung cancer surgery, especially with pre-existing respiratory limitation.

Many lung resections are done by VATS (video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery) or RATS (robot-assisted) through small 1–5 cm cuts under the arm and/or below the shoulder blade, so a large thoracotomy scar is not always present.

After lung cancer treatment, offer an initial specialist follow-up appointment within 6 weeks and regular appointments afterwards; tell people how to contact their clinical nurse specialist between visits.

recall.think: Scar plus focal right upper-zone signs means lobectomy, not pneumonectomy. Stable baseline or new change?
recall.say: “These findings fit a previous right upper lobectomy; I would compare them with the operation note and prior imaging.”
do: Observations → inspect (thoracotomy or VATS scars, symmetry, trachea) → expansion → percussion → auscultation, always comparing both sides.

numbers.meaning: No fixed diagnostic threshold. Scenario observations: interpret with baseline.

recall.trap: Interpreting post-lobectomy changes as a pneumonectomy, or dismissing a new respiratory problem as expected postoperative breathlessness.
recall.finish: Sudden or severe change means urgent assessment (observations, chest X-ray, senior review); questions about recurrence go to the planned oncology follow-up.

partner.opening: Perform a focused respiratory examination, summarise the findings, and outline further assessment if the breathlessness worsens.
partner.actorBrief: Opening: “I get a bit short of breath walking up hills, but it has been much the same since my operation.” Only answer when asked: operation right upper lobectomy eight months ago; breathing at rest comfortable; no fever, productive cough, haemoptysis or pleuritic chest pain; walking distance stable. Do not volunteer surgical type before asked.

reveals.finding: Patient is comfortable at rest, RR 17/min, SpO₂ 96% on room air, pulse 78/min, afebrile.
Mild reduction of right upper chest expansion and breath sounds in the right upper zone; no new focal crackles, wheeze or stridor; trachea central.

reveals.trigger: If the operation is asked about
reveals.finding: Prior operation is RIGHT UPPER LOBECTOMY, not pneumonectomy.
Examiner gives the case examination observations only when each examination step is requested.

curveballs.prompt: Curveball at ~minute 6, after candidate interpretation: “What if I became much more breathless tonight?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: if acute hypothetical, no fresh values are supplied and candidate must call for urgent assessment.
